questions.q: What is the programme mainly about?
options: Why air travel has become so cheap in recent years
How to reduce traffic on the way to work
New ideas that could change future travel
The history of the horse and cart in cities
questions.why: Rob and Neil discuss the future of transport, including driverless vehicles and the Hyperloop.

questions.q: How does Rob answer the question about travelling to work in 30 years?
options: He expects to fly to work
He thinks he will take a driverless car
He says he will still take the train
He hopes he won't be working by then
questions.why: Rob says homeworking will be more common, and he hopes he won't be working in 30 years' time.

questions.q: What is the French company Alstom planning to do?
options: Test goods trains that can run without a driver
Build the world's fastest passenger train
Stop using computers to drive its trains
Make flying cars for city travel
questions.why: Alstom plans to test automated freight trains that can travel about 100 km without a driver.

questions.q: How does Rob first react to the idea of travelling at 1,123 km per hour?
options: He is excited and wants to try it
He thinks it sounds hard to believe
He says it is already common in Japan
He worries that it is too expensive
questions.why: Rob says it sounds 'a bit far-fetched', like flying cars in sci-fi films.

questions.q: How does the Hyperloop One work?
options: Cars drive themselves along special motorways
Planes fly very high above the clouds
Trains run on normal rails with stronger engines
Passengers ride in pods pushed through a metal tube
questions.why: Neil explains you are loaded into a pod and pushed through a metal tube at high speed.

questions.q: Why does Anita Sengupta compare the Hyperloop to planes and maglev trains?
options: To show it just combines two things people accept
To explain why a ticket will cost more than flying
To show that it is slower than a plane on long trips
To admit that it is quite dangerous for passengers
questions.why: She says people have no problem with planes or maglev trains, and the Hyperloop just combines the two.

questions.q: What does BBC correspondent Rory Cellan-Jones think?
options: The Hyperloop will be ready within a year
The Hyperloop uses too much energy
Governments may not agree to build the long tubes
Passengers will be too scared to use it
questions.why: He thinks it will be hard to convince governments to allow long metal tubes on or below ground.

questions.q: What is Neil's view about new transport technology?
options: It is mostly a waste of money
We need to try it, or we would never make progress
It should only be used for goods, not people
It is less important than working from home
questions.why: Neil says we have to try new technologies, or we'd still be travelling by horse and cart.
